description: We're all about space, engineering, AI, cyber security, physics, and ambitious ideas that think out-of-bounds. We look for people who make, tinker, test assumptions, and turn outlandish ideas into real systems. We seek curious engineers, scientists, designers and hackers who have an impressive set of technical skills, a scientist's approach, a creative mind or a passion for tackling tough problems.
summary:
We built Ektos, a tool that lets you compare the same patch of the SPHEREx sky on two different dates. You type a coordinate, and you can blink the two frames, subtract them, or see one date with each eye in a VR headset. An object that moved is easy to spot.

SPHEREx never repeats a wavelength, so there are no ready frames to compare. Ektos builds them from a wavelength range you choose and adds the WISE image from 2010, which gives a 16-year baseline. A color filter removes normal stars and leaves cold objects. 

We tested it on known objects. It measured the 129.5 arcsecond motion of the brown dwarf WISE 0855-0714, and it marked 37 of 42 known cold dwarfs without knowing where they were. This matters because many cold dwarfs near the Galactic plane are still missing, and SPHEREx adds a new date every six months.
details:
Ektos is a tool for looking at the SPHEREx sky the old way by eye. You type a sky coordinate and it shows you the same small patch of sky on two different dates. You can blink between them, subtract one from the other, or put on a VR headset and see one date with each eye. If something moved, you notice it quickly. Pluto was found like this in 1930, and we wanted to try the same idea on SPHEREx.

The hard part is that SPHEREx never takes the same picture twice. Each exposure sees a point of the sky at a different wavelength, so there are no two frames you can compare directly. We solved this by building the frames ourselves. You pick a wavelength range, and Ektos collects all the exposures in that range and stacks them into one frame per visit. It downloads only the pixels it needs, so a field costs about 29mb. The official cutout service sends 1.4gb for the same field. We also put the WISE image from 2010 on the same grid, which gives us 16 years between the first and the last frame. A color filter then removes normal stars, and cold objects are left.

We tested it on objects that are already known. For the brown dwarf WISE 0855-0714 we measured a shift of 129.5 ± 0.3 arcseconds in 16 years. Its proper motion came out as -8.125 arcsec per year, and the published value is -8.118. Then we hid the positions of 42 known cold dwarfs from the tool, and it still marked 37 of them. We repeat every measurement on empty sky as a control. One candidate, SMDET-1, did not pass this check (8.6% chance probability) and we say so in the repository.

We think this is useful because anyone can check a SPHEREx position in a browser, with real data and a small download. Many cold dwarfs near the Galactic plane are still missing. SPHEREx scans the sky again every six months, so each new release gives the tool one more date to compare. We wrote the engine in python with numpy, scipy and astropy. The browser part is plain javascript with webxr and three js. We used an HTC vive pro for the VR scene. The data comes from SPHEREx, WISE and Gaia through the NASA, IPAC archive. The python code and the browser code do the same calculation, and we compared them in 68 checks. All 68 agree.
